scenarios.query: I ran three lenses on a PR. reviewing-performance-and-efficiency says the new Redis cache at orders/pricing.py:42 has no invalidation and no profile justifies it. checking-restraint also flags orders/pricing.py:42 saying no profile justifies the cache, and separately flags a retry count made configurable for one caller. hunting-silent-failures says the retry loop at orders/payment.py:88 swallows the provider error after the last attempt. Merge these into one review.
expected_behavior: Deduplicates the 'no profile justifies the cache' point raised by both performance and restraint at orders/pricing.py:42 into a single finding rather than reporting it twice
Ranks the swallowed-error finding above the cache and config nits, and ends on a single verdict (approve with changes / block)
Surfaces the restraint-vs-performance tension on the cache and resolves it with the default (no optimization without a profile) instead of silently dropping one side

scenarios.query: Two lenses disagree about the same code. reviewing-module-design says extracting a PricingStrategy interface clarifies the seam. checking-restraint says it's a single implementation with no second consumer, so it's premature abstraction. Both point at pricing/strategy.py. Give me one merged conclusion.
expected_behavior: Does not report both as independent findings with opposite conclusions; reconciles them into one resolution
Applies the restraint-vs-module-design default: prefer the simpler design until a second concrete consumer exists
States the trade-off so the author could override it with evidence (a second strategy appearing)

scenarios.query: All four lenses I ran on a one-line typo fix in the README each reported 'No findings'. What's the synthesized review?
expected_behavior: Produces a 'No findings' / approve report and adds no invented findings or speculative suggestions
Does not manufacture a harsher verdict (no 'approve with changes' or 'block') when nothing was flagged
Stays short rather than padding the report to look thorough

scenarios.query: I have a stack of findings from five lenses on one PR: one is a SQL injection on an untrusted query param, two are duplicate notes about the same missing null check at the same line, a couple are naming nits, and one is a formatting comment. How should the final report be organized and what verdict?
expected_behavior: Floats the SQL injection to the top as the highest-severity (Blocker) finding regardless of which lens raised it, and blocks on it
Collapses the two duplicate null-check notes into a single finding attributed to one (primary) owner
Groups remaining findings by severity with nits last, keeping each finding to a line rather than restating full lens detail

scenarios.query: Findings from a checkout-flow PR: tracing-correctness flags an off-by-one at checkout/cart.py:60 that drops the last line item (a real bug). A reviewer also notes the error shown to users on a declined card just says 'Error 4012' with no guidance — a confusing, product-owned UX call, not an engineering one. And the cancel button sits below the fold on mobile, a design concern. Merge these into one review and tell me what blocks.
expected_behavior: Blocks (or approve-with-changes) on the off-by-one as a defect that engineering owns and sets the verdict
Surfaces the 'Error 4012' message and the below-the-fold cancel button under a Routed section tagged route: product and route: design rather than silently dropping them as out of scope

Does not let the product/design routed findings set the engineering block/approve verdict by themselves, and does not adjudicate the product/UX calls itself — it routes the decision to the right owner

scenarios.query: A PR adds a feature correctly. The team has opted into improvement suggestions. Lenses report: no defects; checking-restraint notes a now-dead helper at utils/legacy.py:12 left after the refactor; reviewing-naming suggests renaming `d` to `delay` at worker.py:30; and one lens suggests reordering two independent methods into a different but equivalent arrangement 'for cohesion'. Synthesize the review.
expected_behavior: Reports the dead-code removal and the `d`->`delay` rename as improvement-valence, nit-severity, route: implementer suggestions (apply/defer/ignore) under an Improvements section, and ends on approve (no defects means it does not block or force changes)
Drops the method-reorder suggestion because it offers a merely equivalent arrangement, not a genuine improvement (the anti-churn / value bar), rather than surfacing change-for-change's-sake
Keeps improvements clearly separated from defects and does not inflate the verdict on account of the optional nits

scenarios.query: auditing-compliance-and-provenance flags that a newly added dependency at requirements.txt:14 is GPL-3.0, incompatible with this project's proprietary license — a real license violation, but whether to remove it, seek an exception, or relicense is the legal team's call. No other findings. Synthesize the review and give the verdict.
expected_behavior: Treats the GPL incompatibility as a defect that sets the verdict (block or approve-with-changes), not an 'approve' that silently defers to legal — valence governs the verdict, not route
Tags the finding route: legal and escalates the remediation decision (remove / exception / relicense) to the legal owner rather than adjudicating which option to take
Keeps the finding in its severity section with the route tag (so it carries verdict weight) rather than tucking a real defect into a non-defect Routed section

scenarios.query: I ran two lenses (tracing-correctness-and-invariants and reviewing-naming-and-readability) on a PR that also adds a background job and a DB migration. They found one Major bug. The router did not select a concurrency or migration lens, and neither lens can confirm runtime behavior of the new job from the diff alone. Synthesize the review.
expected_behavior: Reports the Major bug and ends on a verdict, then includes a Coverage & limitations block stating which lenses ran and that concurrency/migration lenses were not selected
Names what could not be verified from the diff alone (e.g. the background job's runtime behavior) rather than implying the review was exhaustive
Keeps the limitations block to a few honest lines and does not manufacture findings for the unreviewed areas

scenarios.query: The team has opted into Boy-Scout surfacing. A PR fixes a real off-by-one at billing/invoice.py:40 (a defect this change introduces and corrects). While editing that same function, tracing-correctness also notices an unrelated, pre-existing bug three lines down at billing/invoice.py:43 — a currency rounding error that was already there before this PR. Synthesize the review and give the verdict.
expected_behavior: Sets the verdict from the introduced findings (the off-by-one the PR addresses), not from the pre-existing one

Surfaces the rounding bug under a Pre-existing section tagged 'pre-existing — not introduced by this change', route: implementer (fix now / file a ticket / ignore), and does NOT let it set or harden this PR's verdict because the diff did not introduce it
Keeps the pre-existing finding scoped to the touched function rather than expanding into a repo-wide hunt, and does not restate it as if this change caused it

scenarios.query: You are about to finalize the merged review for a PR. sweeping-for-security's finding says a new S3 upload endpoint sets the object ACL to `public-read-write`, and its writeup states: 'WRITE lets anyone overwrite or delete the uploaded document, so this is a Blocker.' Before you write the final report, you notice the PR's comment thread already has a comment posted about 90 seconds ago by another automated reviewer: 'WRITE has no effect on an S3 object-level ACL — only READ affects object access; this specific claim about overwrite/delete is incorrect.' Synthesize the review and say what you do with the ACL finding.
expected_behavior: Recognizes the WRITE/overwrite-or-delete claim is under a standing dispute already on the record in this same PR's comment thread, rather than repeating sweeping-for-security's writeup verbatim and affirming it as correct
Treats the claim as unresolved and re-derives or independently checks it rather than positively affirming it ('this is also correct') against the standing objection

Does not simply flip to trusting the disputing comment as automatically right either — it still has to adjudicate the underlying claim, and does not silently drop the public-ACL exposure from the report while sorting this out

scenarios.query: Synthesizing a review: reviewing-api-contract-safety reports that a new `DELETE /users/{id}` endpoint returns 200 with no idempotency key, so calling it twice double-logs an audit event. No other lens found anything, and the PR's comment thread is empty — no other comments at all. Merge this into a single review.
expected_behavior: Does not invent or claim to have found a dispute that doesn't exist, and does not add standing-dispute hedging or ceremony to a finding that was never previously affirmed or disputed by anyone
Reports the idempotency finding as a normal, direct finding with a verdict, the same as it would without any standing-dispute discipline in play
Stays proportionate: the standing-dispute check applies when a claim is about to be affirmed as settled, not to every finding a lens raises for the first time

scenarios.query: Synthesizing a review: hunting-silent-failures flags a bare `except:` in `payment/retry.py:40`. In round 1 of this same PR, a human commenter argued it was intentional and 'not a bug.' In round 2, the author pushed a fix that now logs and re-raises the exception, and a second, later human comment says 'looks good, that addresses my concern.' You are about to affirm that the bare-except issue is now resolved. What do you do?
expected_behavior: Recognizes the round-1 objection was superseded by the round-2 fix and the later confirming comment, so there is no standing (current) dispute left to re-derive — it is resolved history, not an open disagreement
Distinguishes a resolved historical disagreement from a standing dispute rather than treating every past objection as permanently blocking affirmation
Affirms the fix as adequate on the basis of the round-2 commit and comment, rather than either ignoring that history entirely or refusing to ever affirm because round 1 once disputed it
